title: Are Our Standards Too High? Harvard & Stanford MBAs Tell All
summary: In their first Ask Me Anything episode, Jean and Cherie answer listener questions about dating: their icks, the pettiest reasons they refused a second date, the most romantic gestures they've received, mistakes they repeated in relationships, ghosting, downplaying success while dating, and dating coworkers. Their main takeaways are that icks are a mindset that only appear when you're already not into someone, that romance is about attentive small gestures rather than money, and that dimming yourself to 65 percent for a partner is exhausting and unfair to both people.

ideas.idea: An ick is a mindset: when you genuinely like someone, nothing they do is an ick, and when someone is already on their way out, any small thing becomes one.
ideas.detail: Case study: Cherie's foam Yeezy-style slides ick was 'the slide that broke the camel's back' for a guy already on the way out, while Jean found an ex who slept in mid-calf socks cute because she liked him, and Cherie tolerates tiny no-show socks on the man she is currently dating.

ideas.idea: Cherie's ick is a handsome man who knows he is handsome; she prefers humble men with a 'superhero origin story' who were a bit nerdy or bullied as kids and don't realize they're hot.
ideas.detail: She has dated self-absorbed men who love their own abs: 'we can't both love your abs'; women can think they're hot shit but she doesn't like it when men do.

ideas.idea: Small behaviors on a first date are indicators of larger character traits, so it is fair to refuse a second date over them.
ideas.detail: Cherie declined a second date with a man who said he'd ditch the group on a good powder day, reasoning that a 'selfish skier' who leaves you on the mountain will also leave you at home changing diapers while he golfs; he got defensive when she raised it.

ideas.idea: A man who asks you out should solve basic problems like food on the date; having to pull out Google Maps yourself is an ick.
ideas.detail: Jean had to buy her own chips at a drinks-only venue after the kitchen closed; the sisters say they problem-solve all day for work, their mom and themselves, and in a romantic relationship they want the man to take over and propose three restaurant options.

ideas.idea: The most romantic gestures are acts of service that cost time and thoughtfulness rather than money.
ideas.detail: A finance guy with a demanding schedule bought a Costco cookware set, simmered chicken soup from scratch for four hours while working, and delivered broth, veggies, chicken and pasta in separate Mason jars so Cherie could mix and match while sick; he could have ordered soup but time was the premium.

ideas.idea: Romance is proving you listened and then acting on it to surprise and delight, repeatedly, not just once.
ideas.detail: A man Jean dated showed up with a wrapped early edition of her favorite play 'Our Town' after she mentioned it casually, and DoorDashed a bouquet the morning after she joked 'where are my flowers?'; people want to feel seen, understood and appreciated, which are precursors to romantic love.

ideas.idea: Dimming your light to be a 65 percent version of yourself for a partner is exhausting and creates a negative flywheel where they fall in love with a version of you that isn't you.
ideas.detail: Two of Cherie's exes laughed derisively at her ambitions and jokes, so she hid parts of herself to keep emotionally satisfying relationships going; the sisters say this also dupes the partner unfairly, and Jean links repressing yourself to inflammation and physical symptoms via the mind-body axis.

ideas.idea: Ghosting means purposefully ignoring someone you have actually gone on dates with; stopping a dating-app chat before meeting carries no responsibility, like passing someone on the street.
ideas.detail: Cherie regrets 'shirking' an older guy in college instead of saying she wasn't interested, which would have been the bigger-person move; Jean was told years later by a friend's new boyfriend that she had stopped answering him on an app and had no memory of it.

ideas.idea: Being turned off by a partner's success or profession is a useful filter: such a person is narrow-minded and not the right one for you.
ideas.detail: Cherie admits she downplays being a content creator on Hinge first dates because of misconceptions, especially among SF tech bros versus LA where it is a normal profession; Jean doesn't date strangers, is proud of her career and could not imagine being with someone turned off by it.

ideas.idea: Dating a coworker should be approached with caution, clear boundaries and even a contingency plan for the breakup.
ideas.detail: Both sisters have done it (Jean at Goldman outside her direct group and after Zynga; Cherie at LinkedIn) and it ended in disaster or awkwardness; the anxiety of possibly bumping into an ex in the lobby occupies brain space, and the outcome depends on your personality, coworkers gossiping and company culture.

ideas.idea: Exes who treated you poorly do not get to say they are 'proud' of your later success; you got there despite them, not because of them.
ideas.detail: Cherie compares congratulatory texts from exes who now see her on their For You page to an absent father showing up at graduation; she would name their group chat 'Fans'. She also doesn't stay friends with exes, finding it odd once in a new relationship.

ideas.idea: How a man cares for his feet reflects how he carries himself.
ideas.detail: Jean says feet don't need to be manicured but can't be dirty; Cherie hates tiny no-show socks on men because they grip the foot too tightly and show 'toe cleavage'.
